correctness.rationale: For probability measure on the real sphere, every real f is a+Q with Q=xᵀAx trace-free. Gaussian cumulants and polar normalization give EQ²=2p₂/[n(n+2)], EQ³=8p₃/[n(n+2)(n+4)], and EQ⁴=(12p₂²+48p₄)/[n(n+2)(n+4)(n+6)]. At fixed zero sum and p₂, cubic stationarity allows at most two values, whose multiplicities k,n−k give the largest absolute cubic only at a one-outlier spectrum when n≥3. Quartic stationarity allows at most three values; if there are three, the constrained second derivative on a split of a repeated extreme eigenvalue is positive, so both extremes are simple. The zero sum of the cubic roots and the trace condition then force the middle value to be zero for n≥4, giving p₄/p₂²=1/2, below the two-valued one-outlier maximum. For n=2,3 this ratio is identically 1/2. The resulting moment bounds are attained together by the normalized Y_ω. For r=|a|/||Q||₂, their scalar envelope has the stated derivative and the unique positive maximum by the signs and Descartes’ rule; n=2 gives r=√3/2 and quotient 15/7, while n=4 gives γ=1, δ=3, r=1/2 and quotient 21/5. Both excluded pure-component edges have strictly smaller quotient. Cubic equality with a chosen positive constant selects the positive zonal sign for n≥3; for n=2, either sign of a real quadratic is a rotation of the same zonal form. For a complex function the real/imaginary Cauchy–Schwarz bound has equality only when their squares are proportional (or one part vanishes). Real analyticity on the connected sphere then forces the parts to be proportional. These checks establish the global complex result, rather than relying on the supplied 144-assertion report. The frozen checker was inspected, not executed.

evidence: For n≥3 arbitrary real samples, Sharma–Bhandari give 1+α₃² ≤ α₄ ≤ n/2+(n−3)α₃²/[2(n−2)]. Their consequences (1.4)–(1.5) are |α₃|≤(n−2)/√(n−1) (apply also to the negated sample) and α₄≤(n²−3n+3)/(n−1). The lacunary spherical theorem requires gaps at least three in its least-gap case, and the other spherical Nikolskii source treats degree-asymptotic estimates.

evidence: At maximal |α₃| the upper and lower bounds in (1.14) coincide, so optimal skewness already forces optimal kurtosis and Pearson equality. For a centered, variance-one empirical sample U, equality in α₄≥1+α₃² means E(U²−α₃U−1)²=0, hence at most two sample values. Their multiplicities k,n−k give |α₃|=|n−2k|/√[k(n−k)], maximal only at k=1,n−1, including n=3. Such a one-outlier list attains both endpoints. For n=2 a centered pair has α₃=0, α₄=1 identically.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: The standard moment conversion gives exactly γ_n and δ_n, with simultaneous equality at the positive zonal spectrum. Expanding E(a+Q)^4 now gives the sharp envelope at every nonnegative ratio without solving any additional spectral optimization, and the cubic term for a≠0 forces this same rigidity. A one-variable derivative fixes the optimum and real/imaginary Cauchy–Schwarz with the analytic identity principle fixes the common phase. Thus neither the algebraic number nor the equality law requires a new nonstandard extremal step.

originality.rationale: The exact mixed quotient was not found verbatim, but the decisive joint moment extremum is a direct specialization of Sharma–Bhandari’s finite-population skewness–kurtosis theorem (which also records the classical sharp marginal bounds). Applied to the eigenvalues, that theorem gives both coefficients, their simultaneous equality law, and hence the full sharp mixed scalar envelope by the usual spherical moment conversion. The claimed ratio and rigidity then follow by differentiation and the standard complexification equality step. The failure is demonstrated mathematical implication, not a keyword miss or inaccessible source.
